amendments.why: Rule 14 tells you to read the waw's connective off the ASV, but it says nothing about which of two connective-force words standing together at a clause head is the waw's. That silence is what produced this chapter's only split: `וְעַתָּה` was divided by sense in JOS.14.10 (*And now*) and by word order in JOS.14.12 (*Now therefore*). The added paragraph settles it on the reasoning rule 14 already uses for a correlative pair another morpheme has a claim on, and it contradicts nothing in the corpus, which aligns a waw to *now* in 220 units and to *therefore* in 224 and so attests both words for the waw without saying which it takes when both are written. Everything else in the rule is reproduced unchanged.
amendments.rule: The conjunction `וְ` is normally English *and*, including the waw of a consecutive verb form: the conjunction takes *And* and the verb takes the verb. Where the ASV renders it by some other connective, align it to that word instead. **The list is open and is read off the ASV rather than checked against a set**: the corpus already aligns a waw to *but*, *then*, *so*, *or*, *now*, *also*, *for*, *therefore*, *neither*, *nor*, *yea*, *yet*, *even*, *with*, *moreover* and *howbeit*, among others. A connective the ASV has written for a waw is never `added`, and it is never folded into a neighbouring word to avoid one: a town list writes *with* for the waw of `וְחַצְרֵיהֶן` → *with their villages* and *even* for the waw of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea*, and each waw takes the word written for it. **Where the ASV renders one connective morpheme by a correlative pair such as *both … and*, *either … or* or *whether … or*, both English words belong to that morpheme's one discontinuous unit, headed on the closing connective (*and* or *or*); the opening correlative is not `added`.** **This governs the disjunctive `אוֹ` exactly as it governs a waw**, since what licenses the pair is the one connective the ASV has rendered by it and not the lemma: `לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה` → ***whether*** *a male* ***or*** *a female* gives *whether … or* to the single `אוֹ`, headed on *or*. Where the Hebrew instead writes a connective of its own for each member — `אוֹ … אוֹ` → *either … or* — each takes only the English word written for it and there is no pair to place. **But that governs only a pair no other morpheme has a claim on.** Where another morpheme standing in the clause is itself what the opening correlative says — a present negative for the *neither* of *neither … nor*, the `מִן` of a `מִן … עַד` range for the *both* of *both … and* — that morpheme takes the opening word and the waw takes only the closing connective, exactly as rule 47 gives a written *the* to a present article before a supplied one and rule 46 gives a *that* to a present relative before a bare participle. `אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ הֵמָּה וַאֲבוֹתָם` → *whom* ***neither*** *they* ***nor*** *their fathers have known* gives *neither* to `לֹא` and *nor* to the waw, and `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` → ***both*** *the birds of the heavens* ***and*** *the beasts* gives *both* to `מִן` and *and* to the waw, leaving the `עַד` `unrepresented` under rule 40. **A morpheme that merely stands where the opening correlative stands has no claim on it.** What gives another morpheme that word is that the morpheme is itself what the correlative says, so read sense and not position: the two `לְ`s of `לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה` stand exactly where an English *whether* and a second *for* would stand, and a benefactive preposition is not what *whether* says, so both are `unrepresented` under rule 40 and neither takes the word. Count the correlative's members against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. This does not touch rule 35's fusion, which is a single English word carrying every morpheme's sense: a lone *Nor* or *neither* with no answering *nor* written is that rule's, and only a written pair is this one's. **And a pair is written only where the opening correlative stands before the first member.** Where the ASV instead postposes a floating *both* after the coordinated members, no correlative pair is written and the word is not the waw's: the waw takes the *and* written for it, and the *both* is its own `added` unit under rule 30, for the reason rule 51 gives about a second English word offered to a waw that already holds one. `אֹתוֹ וְאֶת־בְּנוֹ לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ בְּיוֹם אֶחָד` → *ye shall not kill it and its young* ***both*** *in one day* leaves its *both* `added`, while the *both* of `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` above is written where the pair opens and is placed as that sentence directs. Read the English word order, since what tells the two apart is where the ASV has put the opening word and not that it has written one. Read what stands in the clause for that waw in particular, as rule 51 requires for *also*, and where the ASV leaves it unrendered, mark it `unrepresented`. **But read whether a waw is present at all before placing the connective.** Where the ASV writes a coordinating *and*, *or* or *but*, or a resumptive apodosis connective such as *then*, *so* or *therefore*, for a clause or phrase in which no conjunction morpheme stands, no morpheme licenses that word and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30. Hebrew juxtaposes where English coordinates, and the ASV supplies the connective freely: `עַל־כָּתֵף תִשָּׂא בָּעֲלָטָה תוֹצִיא` → *shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulder,* ***and*** *carry it forth in the dark* writes one for a clause the Hebrew leaves asyndetic, and `לְיוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם אֶל־אַדְמַת יִשְׂרָאֵל` → *concerning the inhabitants of Jerusalem* ***and*** *the land of Israel* writes one for a second prepositional phrase the Hebrew merely sets beside the first. Do not fold such a word into the preposition, the verb or the noun standing next to it to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them, and a preposition whose own relation the ASV has left unstated is `unrepresented` under rule 40 rather than a home for a coordinator. Count the clause's conjunctions against the ASV's connectives, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and mark whichever side is in surplus. **The apodosis connective is counted on exactly those terms, and the list of words that can carry it is as open as the connective list above.** Casuistic and temporal law writes its apodosis with a waw as often as without one, and the ASV writes a *then* either way, so read the Hebrew: `וְשָׁמְרוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־מִשְׁמֶרֶת יְהוָה` → ***then*** *the children of Israel kept the charge of Jehovah* gives *then* to the waw written for it, while `עַל־פִּי יְהוָה יַחֲנוּ` → ***then*** *according to the commandment of Jehovah they remained encamped* leaves the same word `added`, because that apodosis is juxtaposed with no conjunction in it at all. Do not give such a *then* to the preposition, the verb or the temporal phrase it stands beside, and do not read a waw the ASV has left unrendered as its home either: where the apodosis writes a waw and the ASV opens the clause bare, that waw is `unrepresented` under this rule's earlier sentence. Read the clause before counting, since a morpheme that has an English word of its own is not made a surplus by this sentence: a present negative carries a *nor* or a *neither* under rule 35, a `כִּי` or an `אִם` carries a *but* or an *or* the ASV has written for it, and only a connective no morpheme answers to is `added`. **And a coordinator standing inside one morpheme's own English rendering is not a connective supplied for the clause at all.** Where the ASV renders a single source morpheme by a fixed English phrase that contains an *and* or an *or*, the word coordinates the parts of that phrase and not two source items, so it belongs to that morpheme's unit, is neither `added` nor a separate connective, and does not move the unit's head, which rule 44 leaves on the lexical verb because a phrasal particle names nothing on its own. Decide it by asking what stands on either side of the English word in the Hebrew, which is the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use and the one rule 30 applies to its one-English-word condition. Where a source clause or phrase stands on each side, the preceding sentences govern and a connective no waw answers to is `added`; where the same one morpheme's rendering runs on both sides and no source item is coordinated at all, the word is written inside that rendering rather than beside it. `וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתוֹךְ אֲרָיוֹ` → *And he went up and down among the lions* keeps *up and down* whole with the one verb it renders, while `אָבְדָה תִקְוָתָהּ` → ***and*** *her hope was lost* leaves its supplied *and* `added`, because there a written clause stands on either side of it. **And where the ASV writes two connective-force words together at a clause head, read which morpheme's own sense each carries before placing either.** Hebrew opens a clause with a waw and a discourse adverb standing side by side — `וְעַתָּה` is the commonest — and the ASV answers the pair with two English words, as *And now*, *Now therefore* or *Wherefore now*. Two English words answer to two morphemes and neither is a surplus, so the adverb takes the word that writes its own lexeme and the waw takes the connective left over, exactly as this rule's correlative sentences give the opening word to a morpheme that is itself what that word says and rule 11 gives a function word first to the morpheme whose sense it carries. `וְעַתָּה הִנֵּה` → ***And now*** *behold* gives *And* to the waw and *now* to `עַתָּה`, and `וְעַתָּה תְּנָה־לִּי` → ***Now therefore*** *give me* gives *Now* to `עַתָּה` and *therefore* to the waw, though the waw's word there stands second. Position is not what decides it, for the reason rule 51 gives about a postposed *also*: the unit is reordered under rule 25 rather than broken, and one chapter may write both shapes, as JOS.14.10 and JOS.14.12 do. Where the ASV writes only one word for such a pair, count as this rule already directs and mark `unrepresented` whichever morpheme it leaves unrendered.

conventions: `וְעַתָּה` at a clause head (vv. 10 twice, 12): `עַתָּה` takes the English *now* wherever the ASV writes one, and the waw takes whatever other connective stands beside it — *And now* in v. 10, *Now therefore* in v. 12, where the waw's word stands second and its unit is reordered under rule 25. Do not divide the pair by the order of the English words.

The idiom `מִלֵּא אַחֲרֵי` → *wholly followed* (vv. 8, 9, 14) is split, not fused: the verb takes the *wholly* and the preposition `אַחַר` takes the *followed*, since the ASV writes an English word for each and rule 2 splits where each morpheme owns one. The subject pronoun goes to the verb under rule 17 where no explicit pronoun stands (vv. 9, 14) and to `אָנֹכִי` where one does (v. 8).

The age idiom `בֶּן` + numeral + `שָׁנָה` (vv. 7, 10) puts the *old* on the construct `בֵּן`, which is also the predicate carrying the verbless clause's supplied copula under rule 20 — *old was* in v. 7, *am old* in v. 10, discontinuous across the numeral phrase — while the numeral and the counted noun keep their own words and an explicit `אָנֹכִי` keeps only its *I*.

Count the clause's conjunctions against the ASV's connectives, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and mark whichever side is in surplus. **The apodosis connective is counted on exactly those terms, and the list of words that can carry it is as open as the connective list above.** Casuistic and temporal law writes its apodosis with a waw as often as without one, and the ASV writes a *then* either way, so read the Hebrew: `וְשָׁמְרוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־מִשְׁמֶרֶת יְהוָה` → ***then*** *the children of Israel kept the charge of Jehovah* gives *then* to the waw written for it, while `עַל־פִּי יְהוָה יַחֲנוּ` → ***then*** *according to the commandment of Jehovah they remained encamped* leaves the same word `added`, because that apodosis is juxtaposed with no conjunction in it at all. Do not give such a *then* to the preposition, the verb or the temporal phrase it stands beside, and do not read a waw the ASV has left unrendered as its home either: where the apodosis writes a waw and the ASV opens the clause bare, that waw is `unrepresented` under this rule's earlier sentence. Read the clause before counting, since a morpheme that has an English word of its own is not made a surplus by this sentence: a present negative carries a *nor* or a *neither* under rule 35, a `כִּי` or an `אִם` carries a *but* or an *or* the ASV has written for it, and only a connective no morpheme answers to is `added`. **And a coordinator standing inside one morpheme's own English rendering is not a connective supplied for the clause at all.** Where the ASV renders a single source morpheme by a fixed English phrase that contains an *and* or an *or*, the word coordinates the parts of that phrase and not two source items, so it belongs to that morpheme's unit, is neither `added` nor a separate connective, and does not move the unit's head, which rule 44 leaves on the lexical verb because a phrasal particle names nothing on its own. Decide it by asking what stands on either side of the English word in the Hebrew, which is the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use and the one rule 30 applies to its one-English-word condition. Where a source clause or phrase stands on each side, the preceding sentences govern and a connective no waw answers to is `added`; where the same one morpheme's rendering runs on both sides and no source item is coordinated at all, the word is written inside that rendering rather than beside it. `וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתוֹךְ אֲרָיוֹ` → *And he went up and down among the lions* keeps *up and down* whole with the one verb it renders, while `אָבְדָה תִקְוָתָהּ` → ***and*** *her hope was lost* leaves its supplied *and* `added`, because there a written clause stands on either side of it. **And where the ASV writes two connective-force words together at a clause head, read which morpheme's own sense each carries before placing either.** Hebrew opens a clause with a waw and a discourse adverb standing side by side — `וְעַתָּה` is the commonest — and the ASV answers the pair with two English words, as *And now*, *Now therefore* or *Wherefore now*. Two English words answer to two morphemes and neither is a surplus, so the adverb takes the word that writes its own lexeme and the waw takes the connective left over, exactly as this rule's correlative sentences give the opening word to a morpheme that is itself what that word says and rule 11 gives a function word first to the morpheme whose sense it carries. `וְעַתָּה הִנֵּה` → ***And now*** *behold* gives *And* to the waw and *now* to `עַתָּה`, and `וְעַתָּה תְּנָה־לִּי` → ***Now therefore*** *give me* gives *Now* to `עַתָּה` and *therefore* to the waw, though the waw's word there stands second. Position is not what decides it, for the reason rule 51 gives about a postposed *also*: the unit is reordered under rule 25 rather than broken, and one chapter may write both shapes, as JOS.14.10 and JOS.14.12 do. Where the ASV writes only one word for such a pair, count as this rule already directs and mark `unrepresented` whichever morpheme it leaves unrendered.
amended.why: Rule 14 tells you to read the waw's connective off the ASV, but it says nothing about which of two connective-force words standing together at a clause head is the waw's. That silence is what produced this chapter's only split: `וְעַתָּה` was divided by sense in JOS.14.10 (*And now*) and by word order in JOS.14.12 (*Now therefore*). The added paragraph settles it on the reasoning rule 14 already uses for a correlative pair another morpheme has a claim on, and it contradicts nothing in the corpus, which aligns a waw to *now* in 220 units and to *therefore* in 224 and so attests both words for the waw without saying which it takes when both are written. Everything else in the rule is reproduced unchanged.

report: Checked all 38 candidate lemma groups, plus the dump read end to end for what the lemma table cannot see: the chapter's single `added` unit and every supplied English word folded into a licensing morpheme.

One genuine split. `וְעַתָּה` at a clause head is analysed two ways: JOS.14.10 writes *And now* and gives *now* to `עַתָּה`, while JOS.14.12 writes *Now therefore* and gives *Now* to the waw and *therefore* to `עַתָּה`. The source is identical in both, and the same English word ends up on different morphemes with nothing in the Hebrew to license the difference. Patched JOS.14.12 to match v. 10: `עַתָּה` takes the *Now* that writes its own lexeme, the waw takes the *therefore* left over, its unit reordered under rule 25. That is rule 14's own correlative carve-out — a morpheme that is itself what the English word says takes it before the waw does — together with rule 11's priority for the morpheme whose sense a function word carries.

Candidates examined and rejected as ASV-licensed rather than splits: `כַּאֲשֶׁר` fused to one *as* in vv. 2, 5, 7, 10, 12 against the correlative *as … as* of v. 11, where the ASV writes two words and both belong to the one connective; the article aligned to *the* elsewhere but `unrepresented` in vv. 9, 10, 12, 14 where a demonstrative pronoun holds the phrase's one determiner (rules 41, 47), against v. 10 s037 and v. 11 s003 where no pronoun stands and the article itself takes the written *this*; `לְ` variously *unto*, *for*, *of* and `unrepresented`, each read off what the ASV writes, with the resultative `לְ` of `הָיָה לְ` silenced identically in vv. 9 and 14 (rule 21) while v. 13, having no `הָיָה`, keeps the *for* written for it; `אֵת` unrepresented throughout except v. 1, where the marker carries the *unto* of *distributed unto them* (rule 16's first family), and v. 12 s037, which is the homograph preposition H854 and carries the predicate's copula under rule 49.

Copula placement is uniform: the construction-supplied copula joins the predicate everywhere it is written — the prepositional predicates of vv. 7 and 11 (rule 49), the adverbial anchors of vv. 11 and 12, the predicate nominals of v. 15, and the `בֶּן` of the age idiom in vv. 7 and 10 — while an explicit subject pronoun keeps only its own word (vv. 6, 7, 8, 10, 12).

The chapter's one `added` unit, the *and* of *cities great and fortified* in v. 12, is right: the Hebrew juxtaposes `גְּדֹלוֹת בְּצֻרוֹת` with no conjunction. Every other supplied English word in the chapter has a morpheme that licenses it, and each was given to that morpheme rather than left `added` — the antecedent *the inheritances* and italic *houses* in v. 1, *the time that* in v. 10, the resumed *it* in v. 7 and *I* in v. 11, *which Arba* in v. 15. That is one policy applied throughout, not two.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. All nineteen are the documented convention difference, where BSB attaches a function morpheme to its host phrase and this project aligns it on its own merits — the ten articles are rule 47's agreement articles and rule 41's determiner cases; the four `לְ`s are rule 27's `לֵאמֹר`, rule 21's resultative and rule 40's bare dative *give me*; the three `אֵת`s are rule 16's ordinary unrepresented marker; the v. 3 `לַ` is left with nothing by the *beyond the Jordan* recasting (rule 40); and the v. 12 `ה` is the cohortative of `תְּנָה`, not a directive `Sd` (rule 32). No accepted edge was changed to move the figure.
Recorded three conventions and one amendment to rule 14, which is the rule that governs the split above and was silent on which of two clause-head connectives belongs to the waw.
